tagline: From Charleston Boulevard to sandstone cliffs, a ranch and a gypsum town
intro: West of Las Vegas, SR 159 changes from the urban Charleston Boulevard corridor to a rural two-lane road curving beneath Red Rock Canyon. The Wilson Cliffs stand to the west, and the road crosses Cottonwood Valley. Approximately 8.8 miles of SR 159 in Red Rock Canyon became a Nevada Scenic Byway on June 30, 1995. BLM highlights the conservation area's red- and cream-colored sandstone cliffs and its hiking and climbing terrain.

Travel through Cottonwood Valley long predates the highway designation. In the mid-1830s, a campsite developed beside the spring-fed creek at what is now Spring Mountain Ranch. Pack and wagon trains used the site until rail travel replaced them in 1905. Farther along the valley, gypsum production brought another change: a wallboard plant opened in 1941, followed by construction of the Blue Diamond company town in 1942. Blue Diamond occupies the site of Cottonwood Spring, a watering place on the Old Spanish Trail and the later Mormon Road.

Driving from the Summerlin South side toward Blue Diamond, the road curves around Red Rock Canyon. The 13-mile Scenic Loop is a separate one-way excursion from SR 159. The ranch lies five miles northwest of the town. Continue toward Spring Mountain Ranch State Park, then Blue Diamond and the junction with SR 160.

moments.title: Red Rock Canyon Scenic Loop
moments.text: The Scenic Loop begins at the visitor center and travels one way for 13 miles. A moderate opening climb gives way to mostly downhill or level driving. Near the northern section, huge sandstone blocks remain from the Excelsior Company's early-20th-century quarry. The operation closed because it was uneconomical. The surrounding cliffs record another kind of movement: the Keystone Thrust forced older gray sedimentary rocks over younger red rocks. That contact is exposed for 13 miles along the escarpment. The Aztec Sandstone began as immense desert dunes, later cemented with calcium carbonate and iron oxides into the rock seen here.

moments.title: Spring Mountain Ranch State Park
moments.text: A spring-fed creek and grassy meadows made this a campsite for travelers on the alternate Spanish Trail route through Cottonwood Valley. Camping began in the mid-1830s; pack and wagon trains continued using the site until the railroad replaced them in 1905. James B. Wilson and George Anderson established Sandstone Ranch in 1876. The cattle ranch later became a retreat. Later owners included Chester Lauck, Vera Krupp and Howard Hughes. The state park preserves the ranch, including its main house, blacksmith's shop, barn, corral and chinchilla shed. The preserved property also includes a cabin, bunkhouse and Wilson family cemetery.
moments.notice: Notice the ranch buildings, including the blacksmith's shop and chinchilla shed.

moments.title: Blue Diamond
moments.text: Blue Diamond grew as a company town after gypsum processing moved closer to the mine. The plant opened in 1941, and the company began building the town the following year. Gypsum mined at the top of Blue Diamond Hill traveled by tram to the processing area at the bottom. The village of Cottonwood briefly became Blue Diamondville before taking the name Blue Diamond later in 1942. Its general store, built in 1942 for a community composed mostly of miners, retains its original exterior appearance. Historical photographs supplied by the Blue Diamond Historical Society hang inside.

practical: Red Rock Canyon Scenic Loop: For the Scenic Loop, a timed-entry reservation is required each day from October 1 through May 31 for entry between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. (checked 2026-10-11)
